literal: Even in the face of the mother who gave birth, [drunkenness] is unpleasant indeed; what then [will it be] in the face of the noble?
translation: If drunkenness is offensive even in the presence of one's own mother, how much more shameful must it be in the presence of the wise and noble?
modern: பெற்ற தாயின் முன்னிலையிலேயே மது மயக்கம் வெறுக்கத்தக்கது என்றால், அறிவு ஒழுக்கங்களில் சிறந்த சான்றோர்களின் முன்னிலையில் அது எவ்வளவு இழிவானதாக இருக்கும்?
explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute disgrace of intoxication by comparing its effect on two highly respected figures: one's mother and the wise. A mother's love is unconditional, yet even she cannot bear to look at her child in a drunken state; it brings her pain and disgust. If the most forgiving person finds it intolerable, the couplet asks rhetorically, how much worse will it appear to the noble and virtuous ('சான்றோர்') who judge by high moral standards? Thus, the poet emphasizes that drunkenness destroys one's dignity in the eyes of everyone, from closest family to society's finest.
